speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the development of the port of Vancouver. I should like to urge the government and the harbours board to press on with their imaginative plans for the development of this port. Meanwhile I would ask the minister and hon. members to ignore some of the criticisms which have been directed against the manner in which the port of Vancouver is operated. I am referring in particular to comments made by certain provincial cabinet ministers in British Columbia.
At the outset I would emphasize the importance of the port of Vancouver. If it is not yet it will soon be the busiest, most productive and most efficient port in this country. As some hon. members have said, it is the busiest port on the west coast of North America. It is busier than Los Angeles, Long Beach, San Francisco and Seattle combined. It is moving more than 20 million tons of cargo this year. The largest port in the world, the port of London, is moving cargos of the order of 60 million tons. In other words, Vancouver already looms large on the world scale. Vancouver is gaining on Montreal. By 1967 or 1968 Vancouver will probably become Canada's busiest and most important port. I have drawn this quick comparison with Montreal because I wish to make certain other comparisons using figures I have extracted from reports of the National Harbours Board. First of all, speaking as a British Columbian I want to say that we in the west do not want to miss out on anything. We are out on the end of a long limb, and we do at times feel we are left out of things-that we should speak out more often and more effectively, particularly in parliament and other places in eastern Canada, in order to get our fair share of federal assistance with respect to national development and expenditure by the harbours board. People out west, in other words, think of the port of Vancouver as being a sort of Cinderella. Her governess has other daughters in eastern Canada of greater age. Though less attractive they have been able, year after year, to get more attention than Vancouver, the Cinderella among our ports.
Here are a few figures to emphasize the point I am making. The capital assets of the port of Montreal are now of the order of $188

million. This figure is taken from the last published report of the National Harbours Board. The capital assets of Vancouver amount to about $58 million. In other words, there has been three times as much invested over the years in Montreal as in Vancouver although, as I have mentioned, the tonnage moved by the two ports is now comparable. From 1956 to 1964 investment in Montreal has been about six times as great as investment in Vancouver. I am speaking, of course, of investment by the National Harbours Board. In other words, despite the comparability of the tonnage moved there has been a much heavier investment by the nation in the port of Montreal and an increasingly heavy bias toward Montreal a bias which I believe is about to be corrected and will be further corrected in the years ahead.
I have looked over the estimates for the current fiscal year. I have glanced too at the estimates tabled today for the year ending March 31, 1967. As I looked over the details on page 517 under the heading "Department of Transport-National Harbours Board" I saw many ports listed as receiving capital assistance toward construction, acquisition of buildings, equipment and so on. I saw reference to such ports as Halifax, Saint John, Quebec and Churchill. These are all ports which will receive investment capital during the coming fiscal year in sums totalling more than $5 million. This money will come out of the general revenue of Canada.
I noticed specifically reference to the area of Montreal. The estimates for 1966-67 also include $544,000 for Expo '67. This year I believe this figure is in the order of $4.8 million. Another item is the Jacques Cartier bridge deficit, $328,000, also paid through the National Harbours Board. These are all items which involve the expenditure of taxpayers' money. They involve taxes which have to be collected currently in order to meet losses in these harbours of eastern Canada.
What were these losses? At Saint John the total was $1.1 millions, at Halifax, $442,000, at Quebec, $700,000, at Montreal, $1 million, at Churchill, $336,000. These figures are for 1964 as reported by the National Harbours Board. But the port of Vancouver, as is typical, made a profit, last year amounting to about $1,500,000. So we have in Vancouver a harbour which handles a volume of shipping comparable with Montreal. It does this on the basis of a federal investment one third of that invested in Montreal. It is a harbour
February 14, 1966

which earns a profit whereas the port of Montreal loses money.
I would suggest that the funds amounting to nearly $20 million which have been accumulated to the credit of the port of Vancouver and put away in Canada Savings Bonds should be invested in new facilities around Vancouver at an increasing tempo. I know that the harbours board in Vancouver has a program providing for the investment of $5 million this year. But I suggest this tempo should be doubled and that an investment in the order of $10 million a year be made for the next five or six years in order to reinforce success.
Vancouver is an efficient harbour. There is no need there for continuous dredging. It does not have a pollution problem like that which the port of Montreal faces. It is thoroughly profitable and it is well run. I should like to underline this fact. The credit balance which has been developing over the years speaks well for the management in Vancouver. Personally I have only the highest praise for the chairman of the board. Mr. Howard Mann is, I think, a perceptive man; he looks a long way ahead. I should also like to congratulate the local port manager, Captain Barney Johnson, who runs a very tight ship. But we still need more imagination, a bolder approach, a more outward-going attitude. I have no doubt that the funds which have been accumulated by Vancouver could earn far more than 4 or 5 per cent. I am confident there are investments to be made in Vancouver itself which will earn 10, 15 or even 20 per cent. Evidence of this can readily be found in the activities of private enterprise in the area.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The harbours board occupies about one third of the waterfront. The remaining two thirds are occupied partly by Indian lands and partly by private corporations. Those corporations have recently been building bulk terminals. Two have already been completed. Both are being expanded and a third very large one will soon be announced for construction on the north shore in my riding. There is also another new grain elevator there. Developments are forging ahead in terms of tens of millions of dollars in investment, and these firms are raising money in competition with other parts of Canada, money on which returns of 10 per cent, 15 per cent or 20 per cent are envisaged.
Supply-Transport
I suggest that the National Harbours Board would do well to match private enterprise development in that area rather than nurse Vancouver along as has been done with some eastern ports. We should do our best through the National Harbours Board to make a complete success of a port which serves all of western Canada, which serves at least a quarter of the people of this country and which serves many industries based on our national resources, be they forest, mineral, agricultural or otherwise.
I should like now to say something briefly about the rates levied in the various harbours across Canada. It has been charged by the minister of industry and commerce of the province of British Columbia specifically that the port rates in Vancouver are three times those in Montreal. This is nonsense. He or certainly his staff, by going carefully through the annual reports of the National Harbours Board, could have found out to the contrary. The facts are essentially that the rates are comparable.
I have made a rough attempt to arrive at figures by summarizing the various charges which have to do with wharfage, docking and dry cargo handling charges, and I came to the conclusion that the average income of the National Harbours Board per ton in Vancouver is of the order of 23 cents and in the port of Montreal is of the order of 26 cents. So in an over-all and very general way the cost is somewhat lower in the port of Vancouver. In other words, the rates are somewhat less there.
I asked for an example of the berthing charges and the National Harbours Board has given me an example indicating again that the berthing charges are less in Vancouver. They tell me that a modern vessel, 550 feet long and of 13,950 net registered tons, in berth from 8 a.m. on Monday morning until 4 p.m. on Friday, would pay $726.70 in Vancouver and in Montreal it would pay $1,778.63 or more than twice as much.
Again I should like to stress that there is a good reason why costs and charges in Vancouver should be less. We have a large harbour provided by nature for the convenience of man. We do not have to spend a lot of money to create such a harbour. In Montreal they are fighting against nature. They are fighting a river. They are fighting low temperatures in wintertime and at the moment at least, they are also fighting; municipalities which have not made adequate:

February 14, 1966
Supply-Transport
arrangements to look after their own pollution problem.
I should like to compare very briefly the charges on the United States west coast with those in Vancouver. Generally speaking they are 15 to 25 per cent higher. In other words, the port of Vancouver levies rates similar to those charged in Montreal and lower rates than those charged on the west coast of the United States. Therefore I do not think we need bow our heads or apologize in any way for the manner in which charges are levied in Vancouver harbour.
I should now like to say a word about forward planning. I have mentioned that the National Harbours Board in Vancouver occupies about a third of the waterfront, that private enterprise occupies a large area, and that increasingly Indian lands are being leased to private corporations for bulk loading plants, new grain elevators and the like. Up to about three years ago the port authority in Vancouver by and large went its own way, and while it endeavoured to answer inquiries from the neighbouring municipalities around the Vancouver area it did this on an ad hoc basis. Its relations with the railways and the various other companies were also on a piecemeal basis.
Then it was decided that we should have more information on the long-term plans, not just of the harbours board, but of the other operators around the harbour, including the much maligned C.P.R., the C.N.R. and so on. After a number of meetings we managed to set up-this was done under the former minister of transport, now Minister of Public Works-the port of Vancouver development committee.
I will briefly run over its terms of reference:
1.	To ensure the preparation and periodic revision of short and long-range development plans for the port of Vancouver, with estimate of capital requirements and economic feasibility.
2.	To ensure that such plans, when endorsed by it, shall be brought to the attention of the public and that appropriate action be taken by the various interests concerned.
3.	To ascertain and advise on priorities for specific projects within the context of such development plans.
4.	To provide a continuing means of liaison between the various economic interests of the port area and the port administration, with respect to both short and long range plans.
The membership of that committee includes the shipping interests, such as the Vancouver Chamber of Shipping, the Vancouver Merchants' Exchange, the railway

companies, the trucking companies, the B.C. Wharf Operators' Association, the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators' Association, the Vancouver Board of Trade, the North Vancouver Chamber of Commerce, the city of Vancouver, the city of North Vancouver, the city of Port Moody, the district of north Vancouver, the district of West Vancouver, the corporation and district of Burnaby and the National Harbours Board. There is also a labour delegate and the National Harbours Board has one representative on the committee of 16.
This port development committee has a budget. The budget is provided under one of the votes of the National Harbours Board. An executive secretary has been appointed together with a small staff, and a number of studies have been commissioned with consulting and other firms. The several studies now under way include a hydraulic model of the harbour to see what dredging, breakwater installations, dock installations and, even causeways might do to the harbour. Another project is a land inventory all around the harbour which will provide a comprehensive review of existing developments, developments under way and others that may be undertaken. A third project is the preparation of a long-term forecast of the traffic volume covering the nature of traffic and how it might ideally be served in terms of new facilities. The committee is also advising, although it does not have the last word, both the minister and the National Harbours Board with respect to the purchase of land for port development projects.
The port development committee is performing a very important function in that it is bringing the most knowledgeable people in the port area together and giving them a forum in which they can table their plans for the future. It gives those on the committee an opportunity to discuss individual plans, and the committee can publish reports on these plans. This it has an opportunity to do on an annual basis. It gives members of the public frequent opportunities to express their reactions to plans and revise their plans so that they are looking ahead in concert with one another.
I should now like to make a protest in this connection. The C.N.R., of course, does a great deal of business in and through the port of Vancouver. About a year ago, out of the blue so to speak, the C.N.R. chose to announce the construction of a tunnel and
February 14, 1966



bridge leading across to the north shore from Vancouver. As a representative of the north shore in parliament I am all for this tunnel and bridge concept. It is long overdue. But certainly a plan of this type should have been brought before and discussed with the port of Vancouver development committee before it was announced in all its detail to the press and public at large.
I think the C.N.R. would do well to co-operate effectively in every way with a consultative agency of the federal government like this port committee, a committee which I am convinced will assist in efficient long-term planning, one which will permit the public and certainly members of parliament like myself and others to understand what developments are under way in the port of Vancouver and what corrective action can be taken in the event of difficulties.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The C.N.R. is in process of building a tunnel costing about $12 million and a bridge costing about $9 million which will reach across to North Vancouver. This will for the first time give the C.N.R. access to the port of Vancouver in its own right without having to go over the rails of the C.P.R. The C.N.R. will have secure operations on the north shore in Vancouver. The C.P.R., as many members know, dominates the south shore. Some individuals have been critical of the fact that the C.P.R. appears to be a vested interest, very difficult to move at times, dominating the south shore. The C.N.R. has a great opportunity to serve the north shore giving proper access to adequate depths of water and so on. The length of the coastline, I can assure you, is just as good in this respect. Soon we will have our two national railways reaching tidewater in the port of Vancouver with their own rail access directly to ocean shipping. These operations will be fully effective within two or three years' time.
I would not refer to highway bridges except for the fact that the federal government, in so far as the port of Vancouver is concerned, has not paid one red cent for highway bridges across Vancouver harbour. There has been some argument about the Second Narrows bridge, but the First Narrows bridge was built by private enterprise and taken over by the government of British Columbia some years ago. The government of British Columbia began to build the Second Narrows bridge in 1957 as a toll bridge. Toll bridges are precluded from being part of the trans-Canada highway by definition. The province of British Columbia, with full knowledge of
Supply-Transport
the consequences of its action decided to build this six lane bridge as a toll bridge and make it self-liquidating. That was the businesslike thing to do in the eyes of that government and it did it. This prevented the federal government forever, unless the Trans-Canada Highway Act is changed, from participating in the financing of that bridge even though it is an integral, physical part of the trans-Canada highway.
I mention this fact because in looking at the reports of the National Harbours Board-I am looking more specifically at the latest one for the year 1964-after the usual accounting of assets and liabilities I find a statement in respect of the profit and loss of the Montreal harbour operation. This shows the annual loss as $1 million. 1 find that the following page deals with the Jacques Cartier bridge at Montreal. It was operated at one time as a toll bridge but the previous government removed the tolls just prior to the 1962 election. These tolls were removed when that bridge was still a long way from being paid for, so the Canadian taxpayers must foot the bill for that bridge with a book value of $24 million and a net loss for 1964 of $683,239.
The next page deals with the Champlain bridge which has an asset book value of $37 million and had a net loss of $1,713,471 for the year 1964. So wrapped up in the Montreal situation so far as the federal taxpayer is concerned is not only the loss of $1 million on the harbour itself but a loss in respect of bridges totalling close to $2,500,000 per year.
We need another crossing over the harbour of Vancouver. One of these days we are going to have to come to the federal authority, if only because the National Harbours Board has a veto in respect of where such a bridge can be located. It must be located in such a way that it will not hamper ships moving in and out of the harbour. It must also be located so that waterfront development is optimum from the point of view of having the right facilities in the right places. I hope and trust that the federal government will participate in the financing of such a crossing and I hope and trust that we will be able to arrange, with the original impetus coming from the province of British Columbia, for a freeway development through the downtown area of the city of Vancouver, with federal assistance for an urban renewal program and so on. With assistance from the National Harbours Board in respect of a freeway development

February 14, 1966
Supp ly-Transport
we will begin to solve our other surface transportation problems as well.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about a passenger terminal and by that I mean a terminal for ocean-going passengers. Vancouver has been used for decades by large passenger ships. Ships currently on world tours still come into the port of Vancouver. They come there to woefully inadequate facilities, ancient facilities, second rate facilities which certainly do not show Vancouver to its full advantage. These facilities are owned by the C.P.R. which loses money in their operation. It could use the same dock space for handling dry cargo and realize another $100,000 per year but it is not economical for the C.P.R. to do so when there is, at least for the current 12 month period, a continuing arrangement with the operators of the ocean liners to the effect that the C.P.R. will permit them to embark and disembark passengers at this point.
I understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway has a very large multimillion dollar real estate development in mind for the downtown area of the port of Vancouver involving downtown Vancouver right along the oldest section of the waterfront for a distance of up to a mile. This involves not just millions but perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars and will include passenger dock complex with stores and a trade centre to display the wares of western Canada thus giving passengers an impression of western Canada as it really is and not as it was 50 or 75 years ago. I understand that the National Harbours Board has been holding discussions with some of the executives of the C.P.R. in this connection, and I trust that this passenger terminal will be an integral part of the port, including a freeway along or close by the waterfront, and that working with the new port of Vancouver development committee the C.P.R. and the National Harbours Board, like the local boards of trade and other interests, will settle on a plan which will be to their mutual advantage and which will shortly begin to take form on the waterfront of Vancouver.
Finally, Mr. Minister, I have seen a reference in the press to the effect that you may be coming to Vancouver. We will welcome you there and we would like to take you around the port of Vancouver. We would like it even better if you could bring some of your colleagues. It would be very pleasant to have the cabinet come to Vancouver to hold one of its meetings there. If the cabinet considered

nothing else than giving the port of Vancouver parity of treatment with the port of Montreal I think this would be in the interests of the people of Vancouver, the province of British Columbia, all of western Canada and, I suggest, the country as a whole, because in Vancouver we have what is going to be Canada's biggest port, what is, already, our most efficient port. I trust that in the forward planning of the National Harbours Board this vision will be kept in mind.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments in this general discussion of the railway transportation system in Canada. I intended to refer in some detail to the box car situation and the movement of grain in the west, but this subject has been specifically covered by a number of members and particularly this afternoon by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose. All I shall say on this subject at this time is that I endorse what those hon. members have said.
We were all very interested this afternoon to hear the minister outline what he referred to as an improvement in the movement of grain during the last few weeks. In this regard I should like to ask why the government waited so long to take action of this kind. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, a former minister of agriculture, advocated the establishment of a committee some months ago. I was in the house when he made such a suggestion but evidently his suggestion has only recently been acted upon. In this regard perhaps I should paraphrase what the Department of Labour has been suggesting: Why wait for spring? That is apparently what has happened in this regard because this problem has continued during the winter months.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I should now like to make a comment or two about the curtailed railway passenger service on the prairies. A few days ago the minister said in the house that the decision of the Board of Transport Commissioners to allow the cancellation of the C.P.R. transcontinental "Dominion" to carry on into the summer would not help him pass his estimates, and he now knows that it has not. However, Mr. Chairman, I think the fact that he has agreed to refer the whole question of railway passenger service to the standing committee on transport and communications will probably shorten this debate, because we intend to make more speeches at that time and go into the details of this subject a little more fully.
February 14, 1966

I should like to put the minister's statement on record. As reported in Hansard of February 4 the minister said:
-we might arrange to have the Canadian Pacific Railway appear before the Standing Committee on Transportation ... to explain what they are doing and proposing to do in connection with their passenger service-
That was just a general statement. Then on February 8, as appears in Hansard-I put this on record because it is a definite commitment and we are sure the minister will live up to it-the minister moved:
That the subject matter of the adequacy of the present program and future plans for passenger service on the lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway to meet the effective demand of the public for such service, and the effects of such program and plans, be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for their consideration and report.
I am very pleased this is going to happen because I represent an area that is on the main line of the C.P.R., namely, the city of Moose Jaw and a large part of the city of Regina. These two cities are very much concerned about the curtailment of railway passenger service and the effect it will have upon the economies of their communities.
In order to impress upon the minister the great concern in western Canada over the fast developing curtailment of railway passenger service I should like to quote one brief statement in a notice by the Civil Service Commission of Canada. I received this notice a few days ago. It is in regard to vacancies in the position of district inspector on railway car equipment. I was impressed by this first statement:
The operating branch of the Board of Transport Commissioners of Canada is concerned primarily with matters relating to adequacy of rail services to the public-
We intend to impress upon the government that we expect them to follow this policy in determining what is needed in regard to passenger services. I should like to repeat what was said by the Civil Service Commission of Canada, that the Board of Transport Commissioners is concerned primarily with the public interest in regard to railway passenger services.
In connection with railway policy, Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer to another statement attributed to the Minister of Transport. He is reported to have said that economic and social factors involved in railway problems should overrule the railways balance sheet. The minister said that in his view that public interest should be put first. These statements
Supply-Transport
put both the Board of Transport Commissioners and the minister on record as supporting a railway policy primarily concerned with public needs.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I represent two important cities that are situated on the main line of the C.P.R. These are only two of eight cities between Calgary and Winnipeg. On January 25 the mayors and aldermen of these eight cities met in Moose Jaw and had a very long discussion. I have here the minutes of their meeting and they fill 12 pages. I shall not inflict them upon this committee or the minister but I should like to give a short summary in this respect. I have read all of the minutes. The delegates were from Winnipeg, Portage la Prairie, Brandon, Regina, Moose Jaw, Swift Current, Medicine Hat and Calgary. They all expressed concern at the curtailment of railway passenger service in western Canada. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am just summarizing the minutes of the meeting.
It was agreed that positive action had to be taken through a meeting with the federal government to emphasize that service to the public should be the main consideration in any railway operation. It was stated that railways were a prime factor in tying western and eastern Canada together. The delegates all agreed that there was need for greater passenger service rather than less. They said it was apparent that the C.P.R. had cut service to the point where no one used the "Dominion" and then had been able to go to the Board of Transport Commissioners and claim that the "Dominion" operation was losing money. To counter this move the delegates agreed that it was necessary to insist that the C.P.R. had undertaken an obligation to the Canadian people when it was given large cash and land grants, on the understanding that it was to efficiently maintain, work and run the railway in perpetuity. The delegates said that the railway should be held to these obligations and responsibilities.
One city official said that the time to fight it out with the C.P.R. was long past and the cities must now take their fight to the federal government. Referring to the Railway Act it was pointed out that the federal government had the power to vary or rescind regulations of the Board of Transport Commissioners. At the end of the Moose Jaw meeting a motion was passed calling for a personal presentation of the whole railway passenger problem to the Prime Minister and his cabinet in Ottawa

February 14, 1966
Supply-Transport
at as early a date as possible. The motion which was passed unanimously, stated that it was apparent that the Board of Transport Commissioners had not weighed the economic and social impact on communities affected by rail passenger service abandonment and had not realistically or objectively assessed the case argued by the communities against such abandonment.
I do not believe a definite date has yet been set for the meeting with the Prime Minister and the cabinet and I should like to suggest to the minister that arrangements be made to hold this meeting at the same time as the inquiry is started by the standing committee of the house.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to interrupt and say I am very grateful to him for saying that because I made exactly the same suggestion to the Prime Minister. I said that I thought the mayors would like to appear before the committee as well as before some of the ministers and that to save them two trips, especially when there are not too many trains to travel on, it would be desirable to hold both at the same time.
I thank the minister for his statement. We are interested in the Prime Minister's reply. Did he indicate that he would take such action?

The Prime Minister indicated that he is quite prepared to see them and has left the date in abeyance at the moment pending arrangements for the setting up of the committee.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

Then, Mr. Chairman, I do not have to impress this upon the minister in view of the fact that he has already suggested it to the Prime Minister. These two meetings should be held at the same time, namely, the meeting with the cabinet and their appearance before the committee. I should like to impress upon the minister the importance of having the meeting of the standing committee as soon as possible so that we can deal with rail passenger service. If adequate transportation facilities are to be provided for summer tourist travel, the question of Canadian Pacific service must be decided within the next few weeks. If the service of the "Dominion" has not been restored this summer, and it appears it is not going to be after the ruling of the Board of Transport Commissioners, at least there should be some form of dayliner

operation to accommodate Calgary to Winnipeg passengers because a considerable number travel between these two points.
I have a transcript of the proceedings before the board on the hearing of the application for discontinuance of the "Dominion". It is a very long document and I certainly will not try to go through it. There are many questions that could be raised about this testimony. It is for this reason I consider it important to have the western city officials at the inquiry to hear the questions and the answers. There will be questions concerning the apparent lack of effort by the Canadian Pacific to encourage passenger traffic. We want to hear the company's answer to the charge that the company has discouraged train travel by inadequate accommodation and equipment. We want to compare the Canadian Pacific passenger policy with that of the Canadian National. It would appear that the operations of the "Dominion" over the last two years compare unfavourably with the Canadian National.
The facts in this regard were brought out in an article in a recent edition of Week End Magazine. The article is entitled, "The Great Passenger Experiment". It makes interesting reading, and I should like to quote one short paragraph to emphasize the point I am making concerning the lack of encouragement given to passenger traffic by the Canadian Pacific:
Under the sceptical but watchful eye of its privately-owned competitor, the Canadian Pacific, the publicly-owned Canadian National is going all out to make the passenger business pay. And to do so it has chosen to apply a classic principle of private enterprise: That the way to drum up business is to improve your product and lower your price.
The C.N. has modernized and speeded up its passenger trains-and it has cut fares. The result: More people rode C.N. trains last year than in any year since world war II. And passenger revenue, after falling ever since the war, is starting to rise again.
As I say, I just read this so that the committee can compare the record of the Canadian Pacific with regard to encouraging passenger traffic with that of the Canadian National. It would appear that Canadian Pacific deliberately curtailed service on the "Dominion" to the point, and I am speaking from experience, where it became unpleasant to travel on it. Prior to 1960 the "Dominion" operated as a conventional, transcontinental passenger train with coaches, diners, sleepers and head-end traffic. When it operated in this fashion the "Dominion" was very well patronized. The "Dominion" service was probably
February 14, I9G6

well maintained up until June, 1965. In the last few months before its discontinuance the "Dominion" had only two coaches and a buffer car for the greater part of the time. Under these circumstances, the railway company should not be able to base its argument on a business loss sustained in the last year or so as the result of curtailed service.
In the judgment to allow the discontinuance of the "Dominion" the Chief Commissioner, Mr. Kerr, said that in his view Section 315 of the Railway Act imposes an obligation on the railway company to furnish adequate and substantial accommodation for the benefit of the public. The Assistant Chief Commissioner, Mr. H. H. Griffin, makes this statement in his judgment allowing the discontinuance:
-in formulating my opinion I have not weighed the economic or social impact on the communities.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this statement is not in line with the statement I read earlier from the Civil Service Commission advertisement. I will read that statement again for emphasis:
The operating branch of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada is concerned primarily with matters relating to adequacy of rail services to the public-
This is all I need to say at this time about passenger service. I should like to refer to one other small item, namely, the slowness of mail service especially with relation to the delivery of daily newspapers from western Canada. I have asked questions in the house in this regard and I have put a question on the Order Paper but have not received an answer yet. I refer, for example, to the Moose Jaw Times-Herald which used to arrive the second day after publication. Last week Monday's edition, in which I was particularly interested, arrived the following Monday, or one week later. I wrote to the publisher of the Times-Herald and I should like to put a brief extract from his letter of reply on the record. He wrote:
In discussing the situation with the local postmaster, I was able to determine that now that the "Dominion" is out of service, truck transit is the only available means of transit.
The papers were, of course, delivered daily to the post office and do leave here on a daily basis. I understand from my discussion with the postmaster that there is a need for transfer at such places as Winnipeg, Fort William and Sudbury going east and Medicine Hat and Calgary going west.
He felt the reason for your receipt of several newspapers on the same day would be a hold-up during transit or even at Ottawa.
Supply-Transport
I just mention that, Mr. Chairman. I have a question on the order paper and I hope to have an answer. I should like to impress upon the minister the fact that there are many side effects of the cancellation of the "Dominion" and the curtailment of passenger service. I give him fair warning that more of them will be brought out at the committee hearing.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I would not want to unduly delay consideration of certain items of the estimates of the Department of Transport, for, if I am not mistaken, we are now discussing sums of money which are already, or will be spent before March 31. Therefore I shall be very brief, and I would simply draw the minister's attention to certain points in connection with the estimates of his department.
There has been much reference to ferry systems across the country to ferry services and port facilities. At this point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote a few remarks in this connection from the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1965. With reference to port facilities, as reported on page 77 of his report, and more particularly in paragraph 122, the Auditor General says:
Continuing federal assistance to intra-provincial ferry services. In our 1963 Report attention was drawn to the continuing federal subsidization of ferry landing facilities for provincial governments despite the general policy of the Department of Public Works and the Treasury Board over many years to regard such facilities at either end of a ferry service linking an intra-provincial highway as the exclusive responsibility of the province concerned.
Further on, he continued:
Construction of the Matane terminal and dredging at Godbout were undertaken at that time on the understanding that the ferry operator would construct the Godbout terminal and acquire and operate the ferry without further federal assistance. Notwithstanding this, executive authority was granted in 1963 for entry into a three-year subsidy agreement.
And he added:
This acquisition has now brought to six the number of locations where the federal government has provided terminals at both ends of crossriver ferry services in the lower St. Lawrence river. The total expenditure over the years for these terminals, which in some cases form part of shipping wharves, had exceeded $7 million at March 31, 1965.
Mr. Chairman, considering these figures and reading this report, I need not tell you

February 14, 1968
Supply-Transport
that I do not agree with the Auditor General when he states that these terry services should be the exclusive responsibility of the provinces.
I know that, in our case, the ferry service between the north shore and the south shore of the St. Lawrence river has been very useful to the people on both shores, and I feel that it should be considered an interprovincial service, because it is also used by people from the Maritimes, not only the passenger service, but also the freight service to ship various products, in particular potatoes from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick as well as dairy products. I should add that this service offers to over half a million people, a means of transportation between the Maritime provinces, the south shore and the north shore.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to add, in passing, that developments on the north shore have been mentioned and that the Auditor General feels that such expenditures are not justified. On the other hand, I would like to call the attention of the house to the publication entitled "The Region with a Future" which contains statistics and says on page 88:

The federal government ought to benefit greatly from the industrial and mining developments on the north shore. On the basis of some $50 million of taxable income the government should obtain about $25 million yearly. Such a revenue would go a long way to compensate the government for whatever expenditure it will have made in the construction of wharves, terminals, icebreakers and for the subsidies it might have granted to ferry services and steamship companies.

I believe this is very significant, Mr. Chairman. And as I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) right in front of me, I hope he is listening carefully and taking note of all these figures.
On February 11, speaking of the estimates for the Department of Transport, the member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) has this to say:
Looking back over the estimates, and knowing the riding well, I believe there are two or three major projects which were to be undertaken immediately after that declaration by the minister. Not one of these projects has been carried out. At Ste Anne des Monts the money voted was intended for the repair of the wharf. Because of the bad state of repair of this wharf the ferry service between Ste Anne des Monts and Sept lies has been discontinued, and any connection we have with the north shore of the St. Lawrence is by means of a detour through Matane.
I should like to tell my colleague from Gaspe that this is not quite true. The service
[Mr. Pascoe.l
between Ste Anne des Monts and Sept lies was dropped precisely because the company claimed it was not profitable. In spite of an annual subsidy of $50,000 granted by the federal government to Ungava Transport Ltd. this company considered the service unprofitable and it was discontinued on November 30 last.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
With regard to this subsidy, I should like to point out to the minister that this amount of $50,000 granted by the maritime commission was most welcome. Of course, I should be very pleased if the commission kept on granting such a subsidy because it could be put to good use in some places of my riding, for instance, for the service between Sept lies and Blanc Sablon, this latter locality with a population of 15,000 people scattered along 450 miles of coast and with little or no service at the present time. I ask the minister to bring pressure to bear on those responsible, so that this amount of $50,000 may be used to improve the service between Sept lies and Blanc Sablon.
Mr. Chairman, I said at the outset of my remarks that I did not want to extend the debate on these estimates. I shall have, no doubt, the opportunity to deal again with the estimates of this department later on and, at that time, I shall have a great deal to say about air transport, shipping, icebreakers, lighthousekeepers, construction of landing strips in remote, isolated and often forgotten areas. I shall certainly have the opportunity to say more.
A while ago, the hon. member for Coast Capilano (Mr. Davis) said that the port of Vancouver was more or less neglected. He also mentioned the tonnage handled there each year. I am aware of the fact that Vancouver has advantages we do not enjoy in the east. On the other hand, I should like to remind him that we too have very active ports in the east. I will mention only one at this time, the port of Sept lies which is rated third in importance, not only in Quebec but in all of Canada. I would like to say to my hon. friend that quite recently, from January 1 to date, winter navigation was never interrupted and without assistance from federal government ice breakers. As our hon. friends often say the icebreakers are used in the lower St. Lawrence, let me say that this year, navigation never stopped, even without the assistance of icebreakers. From Sept lies, third most important port in Canada, and since
February 14, 1966

January 1 only, more than two million tons of iron ore have been shipped. More than 16.5 million tons of iron ore were shipped through that seaport last year, and this is very important, I think.
I wanted to point out those facts because there is a lot of discussion going on here and there, and often in the house, about seaports, the importance of seaports, and the federal assistance they should get. Well, according to the publication "Region with a Future", it is crystal clear that the $25 million collected in taxes by the federal government more than compensate for the work the federal government did or could do in that most important seaport of Saguenay county.
Mr. Chairman, in closing, I would like to say that I hope the minister-I notice that he is taking notes-will not forget the huge developments which are now going on in my constituency and which will continue in the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since it is February 14, St. Valentine's Day, I would assume everything is hearts and flowers with the minister today and I thought he might feel rather disappointed if I did not have a few words to say in reference to his estimates while they are before the house. I wish to say a few words on a subject that is causing me great concern and has caused great concern to the residents of the towns of Sydney Mines, North Sydney and surrounding communities in reference to the situation that exists at the port of North Sydney brought about through the actions of the present administration in regard to the change in plans and mode of shipping goods to the province of Newfoundland.
On many occasions during the last session, right until we adjourned on June 30, I believe, I posed many questions in the house to the Minister of Transport and to the then minister of labour in regard to this matter. Those questions were evaded in every possible way. The ministers always said: Do not worry about this. It is not going to get worse. There will be more employment and everybody will be happy.
We did not have much success in extracting much information from the Minister of Transport or the then minister of labour. However, when we were safely out of here

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion after June 30 the minister concerned issued a press release as to what would happen at the ports of North Sydney in Nova Scotia and Argentia and Port aux Basques in Newfoundland. We find, despite the fact that there was a reply to the question I posed to the minister almost two years ago, that there has been no real answer. As reported in Hansard on page 1359 of March 23, 1964, I asked the Minister of Transport the following:
Is the minister aware that it has been suggested that employment will be reduced by 75 per cent? So it is not too early to start investigating the problem now?
I meant the problem of finding employment for those who would be involved in the releases and cut-backs announced by the government. The minister on that occasion replied:
Experience has been that traffic has grown so much since confederation that employment is always going up, and this is likely to continue if we improve the communications between Newfoundland and the rest of the country.
I fully agree with the minister that freight shipments and so on have been going up every year. However, Mr. Chairman, it would be absolutely impossible to have shipments go up to such an extent as to take up the slack and create the employment which will be needed at the port of North Sydney when the cut-backs take place. Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should issue a white paper outlining with clarity and in succinct terms its views on certain areas of federal-provincial responsibility and, in particular, in order to settle confusion and to enlighten the people, give its opinion on the Question of federal jurisdiction in matters involved in a program of manpower development, the war on poverty including assistance, welfare and family allowances, and corporations and institutions with credit and related functions in their objects and powers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the reasons which persuaded me to put this motion down for debate have an additional urgency imparted to them following the recent scuttling of the Fulton-Favreau formula. It is typical of the strange political world in which we live that this final blow was struck by Mr. Lesage because in its final stages the form of the proposal had been tailored, at least in part, to meet the wishes of the Quebec government after the 1961-62 meetings. I am sure that if the formula could have spoken it would have said "et tu Jean" after he administered the coup de grace.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
For the purpose of this discussion we can forget the merits and demerits of the proposal, though I must say that I made no secret that I had doubts about certain aspects of the formula when the matter was first up for discussion a year ago. But this is beside the point. At least if there had been approval of all parties it would have shown that the provinces and the federal government had developed a real ability to get along together. It would then have been possible to move toward the necessary constitutional changes that the exigencies of the present day demand. But now, weighing the results of the action by Mr. Lesage and his colleagues, it is quite certain that the mistrust and indignation with which at least some of the other provinces will view his stand render it unlikely, if not impossible, that any alternative proposal can be put forward or found acceptable in the foreseeable future.
There should be no doubt that some provinces had reservations about certain terms of the formula. They yielded, however, and set aside their objections in the hope that the mere fact that the 11 governments could have a meeting of minds, a consensus ad
IMr. Speaker.]
February 14, 1968
idem, on a compromise basis on such a contentious issue would augur well for the future. Having done this and made their concessions and now having had the rug pulled out from under them for obvious, pragmatic, political reasons it is sure to be a long time before they come to another conference table and accept any alternative suggestion. So, at this pause in our national journey, when we thought to achieve a new and more modern means of constitutional motive power, we find that all of the careful plans and preparations have gone with the wind and we are back with what we started with so many years ago.
I did not really think we would get the sort of jet propulsion that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has been yearning for in a more material way, but I did think that we might have been able to trade in our team of oxen on a model A, something which would have had marked on it a "made in Canada" label, for the purpose of amending our constitution and effecting changes in the distribution of powers and responsibilities. And I had hoped that because of this there would be a closer liaison and understanding not only between the provinces and the federal government but amongst the provinces themselves.
Thinking Canadians are so deeply concerned about the fact that there are so many areas and so many problems which increasingly will yield only to solution on the basis of co-operation and understanding as well as changes in the distribution of powers and responsibilities. I am thinking of such things as water resources, water pollution, air pollution, agriculture and agricultural rural development and improvement, a national transportation program, manpower development and so on. Thus today we are driven back to the often-used and greatly abused system of federal-provincial conferences as a rough and ready means of working out programs of executive and legislative action in the areas where there must be shifts and changes and co-operation between the governments. This is so because the courts have held that there is no right in the provincial and federal governments to delegate legislative authority each to the other.
It is, of course, possible that the Established Programs Act 1964, otherwise known as the so-called opting out legislation, can be modified and extended to cover additional areas. But this applies, of course, only to
February 14, 1966

cases where the subject matter is under provincial jurisdiction, and financial and other aid is required from the federal treasury, and joint programs thereby emerge. In addition, the service to be provided under the sole administration of the province must be of a similar kind as that which was carried out jointly by the two governments.
To most of us this understanding of the opting out arrangement seems very clear and very definite, but not to the somewhat mildewed, slightly aging pseudo-revolutionaries who, from their vantage points in the seat of government in the province of Quebec, are shrilling out their demands to opt out in family allowances, unemployment insurance, for example, and in other matters where the federal government has occupied the field either under specific power or under general authority.
How can they opt out when they were never in and were never in these fields because they are matters of federal responsibility? I suggest it is not so much a matter of their opting out as their attempting to muscle in. Then there are demands in connection with the conduct of external affairs, the right to deal with banking through alleged control of near banks and so many other instances, none of which could ever be the subject of a true opting out agreement because they were never matters over which the provincial governments had jurisdiction. Surely the Liberal government at Ottawa must realize that many of the proposals which it has advocated, some of which are included in the Speech from the Throne and others which have been discussed, will all wither on the vine if Quebec initially and other provinces later are allowed to trespass on and occupy these fields.
I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that the impression created in the minds of the people of Canada from watching most federal-provincial conferences in the past two or three years has been that of weak, fumbling, federal participation, not knowing what it wants and where it is going, quite prepared to surrender in most things merely to obtain unanimous concurrence in a final communique which applauds the "frank and fruitful" discussions but does not add up the spoils which have been taken away. The picture which comes through of one party is that of a poor pitiful caricature of a government. This contrasts with what appear to be strong provincial delegations, very aggressive, very knowledgeable and very demanding and,
Dominion-Provincial Relations of course, in some instances, very unreasonable and quite prepared to sacrifice the national welfare for regional interests.
One can quite properly suggest here, at least parenthetically, that the proposal that many of these conferences be open and be fully and adequately reported by the media of public information should be accepted. Let there be no doubt that, in my opinion, by far the worst offenders have been some of the leaders of the government of Quebec whose intransigent, provocative attitude, particularly in recent months, has indicated an arrogant disregard of the national interest. This is not an attack on Quebec or the people of Quebec. Some of the other provinces have from time to time asserted claims which cannot be conceded. But it is most unfortunate that it has been some of the Quebec leaders, making what seemed to be the most unreasonable demands, who have caught the attention of the people of Canada by their actions in doing so.
But in this are they acting in the best interests of the people of Quebec? I do not think so. Messrs. Kierans, Levesque, Wagner and others have become so enamoured with the sound of their own voices that they seem to have forgotten the purpose and the meaning and the real objective of the movement in Quebec which so many of us have watched with approval and applause. They have become so obsessed with the means that they have forgotten the end which ought to be achieved. Even if we discount much of what Mr. Levesque said on his last appearance in Ottawa and even accepting the fact that since he has been in public life he has rarely had an unuttered thought, nevertheless we can only conclude that his approach to the course he would have the province pursue can be compared to the phrase coined by railway companies about the advantage of rail passenger travel -"getting there is half the fun".
This is an opportune time to deal with the argument strongly and frequently advanced that all that is being done, all of the claims which are being made can be justified because Quebec is not a province like the other provinces. This is quite true in one sense in which the phrase is used and to that extent I accept wholeheartedly the implications.
Confederation came about and the constitution took the shape it did because in very considerable part an attempt was made to preserve certain characteristics of the inhabitants of Quebec, including a distinct people,
February 14, 1966

Dominion-Provincial Relations culture, civil law, language and so on. To maintain this distinction and preserve and strengthen these characteristics is natural and proper and should receive support from all Canadians. There is, then, some justification for contending that this is one way in which Canada, the nation, differs from our neighbour to the south.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
In this sense there can be no doubt at all about the uniqueness of Quebec and their right to have, within the limitations I have mentioned, the powers it requires to be unique. But when those who use this phrase attempt to stretch it to include an argument of a different kind, when they say that Quebec is not a province like the other provinces and this per se justifies substantial increases in provincial economic and other powers which are consistent only with national sovereignty, then they are attributing a meaning to the phrase which is unacceptable.
In the same way could it not be argued just as easily that the province of British Columbia, remote from the rest of Canada behind the Rocky Mountain wall, with natural lines of communication to the south with the Americans of the Pacific States, is not a province like the other provinces? The prairie provinces, which experience adverse effects from a national transportation system that has made them the victims of a series of horizontal freight rate increases, as well as being subject to the evils which arise from the people of these provinces being the low man on the tariff totem pole, could also be characterized as provinces not like the rest. The Atlantic provinces, which as a result of Confederation were cut off from their natural markets in the New England states and which also suffer from problems of high transport costs, are provinces unlike the others.
If all of these were to contend, as does Quebec, that because of their very distinct positions they too are provinces which are different, that they too are entitled to trespass on the rights which have been given to the nation of Canada, they could make out just as effective, just as sound a case. If this were done, then we would find that the sum total, the aggregate of all the powers and responsibilities given to all these provinces because they are different, would be so substantial, so all encompassing, that there would be nothing left upon which to found a nation. Thus, when this phrase is used in this way it is deceiving, it is improper, and it must be

rejected. And so for these reasons it becomes our duty in this house to do what we can to strengthen the federal government in its confrontations at these conferences, to give it courage and determination.
It is because of this that I have proposed this resolution to urge the government to incorporate in a white paper its views vis-avis federal-provincial relations, including a clear outline of the position the government takes or should take in areas of federal jurisdiction which must not be and cannot be whittled away. These must be asserted positively although not provocatively. This white paper should be prepared and filed as a caveat so that all may take heed and govern themselves accordingly.
The federal government must reaffirm its rights under the specific established powers of the constitution and in addition might well seek a review in certain areas where Privy Council decisions in the past have deprived the federal authority of jurisdiction which it can well be argued was intended for it by the Fathers of Confederation. Some of the earlier decisions dealing with rights under the peace, order and good government clause and trade and commerce are examples. The principle of stare decisis should not apply in constitutional, legal decision-making. There is no reason why the Supreme Court of Canada could not feel free to review and alter these decisions or for the government to ask it to do so.
In such matters as family allowance payments, for example, the federal government has a very wide scope through exercise of the general taxing power and the right to distribute the resulting funds to the people of Canada. The government can also draw comfort from what is known as the growing tree principle, a phrase which appeals to me very much. One of the learned judges said that the B.N.A. Act planted in Canada a living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits. This could apply to banks and banking, as a Privy Council decision in connection with Alberta's Social Credit legislation has already indicated.
Let the government of Canada take the initiative for once. Let them be strong, decisive and resolute. Who knows, they might even seize upon this as an opportunity to test the bold and excite the daring. I am sure if they do so they will secure from many members, certainly from me, such measure of support as they may require.
On an issue of this kind, they will not be a minority government and, Mr. Speaker, they

were not a minority government before the last election on an issue of this kind. The Prime Minister called that election declaring that he required a majority government to help him in his confrontations with the provinces. On an issue of this kind, I am quite confident he would always have a majority to support him. In any event, I made my position clear on this matter both before and during the election and I have not changed since.
Surely on a matter so important and crucial as this there can be no politics and no partisanship in this house. On this matter we cease to be Liberals or Conservatives or N.D.P. or Social Crediters or Creditistes; we are and we must act only as Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion asks the federal government to issue a white paper putting forward policy regarding federal-provincial responsibility in certain areas, namely, (1) manpower development, (2) the war on poverty including assistance, welfare and family allowances and (3) corporations and other institutions in the credit business. The three general areas mentioned, or the six if we include the subheadings under "war on poverty", are not explicitly mentioned in the divisions of jurisdiction under our present constitution.
With respect to manpower, whatever may be its definition it is not mentioned at all in the constitution. "War on poverty" is a phrase coined in the United States and has reference there to a comprehensive program for social and economic opportunity. Its purpose has been the elimination of poverty rather than stopgap periodic assistance. Sections 92(7) and (13) of our constitution refer to charities, civil rights, etc. and these sections have been interpreted to include wider programs of welfare and social security, but no consideration to date has even been given to a program as broad as the U.S. war on poverty.
Sections 91(2), (15) (16) and (19) cover trade and commerce, banks and interest, and the trade and commerce section has been interpreted to include the incorporation of companies irrespective of objects which would include companies in the credit business.
The significant thing in all these areas is that they have aspects which could fall under both federal and provincial jurisdiction. This is a natural phenomenon. In our modern complex world, human creation and conduct
are not easily categorized and certainly are not easily fitted into jurisdictional slots conceived 100 years ago. There are a few problems and needs today which can be approached and dealt with adequately under any one area of legislative jurisdiction. As a result of this situation most federal states have resorted to what is known as co-operative or creative federalism. Several areas of government, federal, provincial and even municipal, get together to attack a problem which because of its many legislative aspects could not be attacked alone.
In a federal system this approach is much more efficient and beneficial than one where the different levels battle for jurisdiction in the courts and elsewhere, although sometimes this will be the last necessary resort. It must be remembered that a constitution is meant to serve the political, economic and social needs of the people and is not to be used in political power plays for the political aggrandizement of politicians.
In the Speech from the Throne we have two references to the manpower department. It says that the manpower department is to be a conversion of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and that the government will develop manpower policies which are essential to the sustained growth of a highly productive economy and to the elimination of pockets of poverty. There is no direct use of the phrase "war on poverty" but job retraining and mobility, education and rural reform have all been described by this term.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
It is doubtful that anyone could speculate as to all the possible legislation that might be enacted under a manpower or poverty administration. Some projects may be clearly federal, others provincial and others questionable. I can see no objection to the government issuing a white paper indicating the general jurisdictional bases for these matters and I think this would be good, but I think it would be impossible to set out with any finality the strict lines of constitutional jurisdiction that this motion demands, especially under our present constitution which in my opinion is extremely inadequate.
It seems to me that we do require a broad and deep study of federal-provincial jurisdiction and the whole role and purpose of federalism in Canada, but such a study should consider all areas of jurisdiction and should be done by a committee of this house
February 14, 1966

Dominion-Provincial Relations or by a royal commission rather than by a white paper. Such a committee or royal commission would be desirable before any wide-ranging constitutional amendment. It is to be noted that the province of Quebec has already established a similar commission.
While we are discussing problems of federalism and the concept of co-operative federalism, I should like to make a few observations regarding some of our recent federal difficulties. As a Quebecker whose principal language is English I consider these questions of utmost importance. My family has lived in Montreal for at least four generations and I consider it my home. I think it is a great and exciting city and I would not consider living anywhere else. However, in recent years there are some in Quebec who act and talk as if everything within the territory of Quebec, including Montreal, is for the benefit of and within the sovereignty of Quebec. In opposition to this view there are many who consider Montreal as much Canadian as it is Quebec. Most of the great economic and cultural institutions which helped build Montreal serve all Canada, not just Quebec. They were built by Canadians of all provinces to serve Canadians of all provinces. I refer to Montreal's port, its railroads, air lines, banks, universities, industries, hospitals and many other things.
These institutions and this city should belong to all Canadians both French and English. I realize this was not always the case in the past when our economic and cultural institutions were not only controlled by English Canadians but by certain established groups of English Canadians, to which my family did not belong, I may say. The solution to this situation, however, is not to transfer control from one nationalistic minority to another nationalistic minority. With this in mind many of us in Montreal are beginning to wonder whether the trend to increasing provincial jurisdiction in Quebec will not lead to injustice for its minorities and stifle the effectiveness of Canadian institutions which are situated in that province. It would seem to me that works and institutions which are interprovincial and which serve people beyond the boundaries of a province should be subject to federal jurisdiction, which does not mean English Canadian jurisdiction or a jurisdiction dominated by English Canada. There are several articles of the constitution which would support this view.

It has been rather disturbing in recent days to hear provincial governments state that they feel they have some sovereign right to share in economic and fiscal policy. These are the same governments which would become immediately disturbed if the federal government dared cross in the most minor way the boundaries of provincial jurisdiction. Sections 91(2), 91(3), 91(14), 91(15), 91(19) and 91(20) of the B.N.A Act clearly give the federal government sovereign authority in determining national economic and fiscal policy. This is not an area with several aspects which require co-operative federalism, although this is not to say that it could not be approached in that way. Until the constitution is amended it must be repected on both sides and, where the job requires, worked out co-operatively by both sides.
In an editorial appearing in Saturday's Le Devoir the editor, Claude Ryan, made the following statement in an article which was entitled:

The English speaking community in the Quebec of today.

At another place he said:

In private life, the last few years have revealed numerous situations in which the minority wields excessive power over the majority.

He says at another place:

The prime responsibility of the English speaking group is to open wide the doors of its institutions to the members and values of the majority, so that they might become, instead of ghettos of power, true expressions of the environment in which they exist.

Mr. Speaker, I agree fully with these statements but I would also suggest that this could be done without weakening the federal authority.
At another place when discussing the role of the English speaking Quebecker in the public life of Quebec Mr. Ryan referred to Mr. Kierans, the Quebec minister of health and welfare, and said:

Instead of considering himself as the "professional defender" of the rights of a small group, right from the start he asserted himself as a Quebec citizen and a Quebec politician. He espoused the over-all problem of the society in which he lives.
February 14, 1966



Once again I would agree with that statement, since Mr. Kierans was elected to the Quebec legislature. But members of parliament elected to the Canadian parliament, even from Quebec, are elected as Canadian citizens in a Canadian milieu to propose Canadian programs.
In concluding his article Mr. Ryan said:

In the difficult phase before us, we must avoid, on the one hand, panic action and, on the other, blackmail. Between those two extremes, men of good will are bound to find the right formula to get us all out of the vicious circle where we have been for many generations.

Again I agree fully with this high principle but I must make the comment that this must apply to Quebec and to the other provinces as well as to the federal government.
